proposals.label: AI risks deepening inequality for Africa
proposals.definition: Concern that AI may exacerbate inequalities or leave developing/African countries as mere users rather than decision makers, with calls for inclusion.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages warning that AI could widen divides, or demanding developing countries shape AI governance rather than only consume it.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude passages about economic inequality with no link to AI or digital technology.
proposals.boundary_cases: Mentions of 'digital sovereignty' or technology as 'instrument of domination' may also fit AI_SOVEREIGNTY_CONCENTRATION.

examples.quote: these technological advances can also exacerbate existing divides if their development as well as access to them remain unevenly distributed
a governance of AI in which developing countries decide instead of simply being users

proposals.label: Technology as instrument of domination
proposals.definition: Concern that AI and technological progress could become a tool of domination, with calls for African digital sovereignty.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages warning against technological domination or asserting digital sovereignty in the context of AI.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude general sovereignty claims about sanctions or politics without technology link.
proposals.boundary_cases: If the passage only speaks of unequal access without domination/sovereignty language, code AI_DIGITAL_DIVIDE instead.

examples.quote: Technological progress must not become a new instrument of domination. Africa must also be a center of creativity, innovation, and digital sovereignty.

proposals.label: AI as source of hopes and fears
proposals.definition: AI explicitly framed as both promising and threatening.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages that pair AI's promise with its threats or abuses in the same breath.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude purely positive or purely negative mentions.
proposals.boundary_cases: Mild hedges ('opportunities ... however divides') count if both sides are explicit.

examples.quote: Artificial intelligence holds great promise for our societies, but it can also pose a number of threats and lead to abuses
a source of many hopes and fears

proposals.label: AI listed among transformations or investment areas
proposals.definition: AI is named in a list of sectors, challenges or transformations without substantive discussion.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages where AI appears only as an item in a list (e.g., invest in education, health, AI) or as a brief contextual remark about transformation.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude passages that develop an argument about AI governance, risk or inclusion.
proposals.boundary_cases: A one-sentence descriptive remark that AI is transforming work and education, with no further claim, counts here.

examples.quote: we need to invest massively in education, in health, agriculture, infrastructure, new technologies, artificial intelligence, inter alia.
AI is already transforming knowledge, work, our economies, education and information.

proposals.label: North-South digital divide including AI access
proposals.definition: Unequal access to the internet and AI between rich and developing (especially African) countries, with calls to bridge the digital divide.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages demanding universal, affordable access to internet/AI or describing a widening North-South gap.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude passages about AI governance or risks without access content.
proposals.boundary_cases: If AI is mentioned only as part of internet access, still code here when the argument concerns the divide.

examples.quote: it is becoming imperative for all countries to have access to the Internet, including artificial intelligence, which is revolutionizing the world as we speak
the so-called spider web favours rich countries while developing countries are still poorly connected, particularly in Africa

proposals.label: Concentrated AI rule-making widens inequality
proposals.definition: Concern that AI infrastructure, knowledge and rule-making concentrated in a few countries will widen inequality, with developing nations demanding a role in setting standards.
proposals.inclusion: Passages warning about AI concentration in a few countries or demanding developing-country participation in AI standard-setting.
proposals.exclusion: General statements of AI benefit without concentration or participation claims.
proposals.boundary_cases: Overlaps with digital divide; code here when concentration of rule-making or infrastructure is explicit.

examples.quote: It can also widen the inequality if infrastructure, knowledge, and rule-making remains concentrated in a few countries.
Developing nations must help shape the standards that will govern technologies affecting their people.

proposals.label: AI improving education, health, agriculture
proposals.definition: AI presented as able to improve sectors such as education, health, agriculture and public administration, and to accelerate development.
proposals.inclusion: Passages listing development sectors AI can improve or opportunities to accelerate development.
proposals.exclusion: Passages only about risk or governance.
proposals.boundary_cases: Development benefit framed within a GDC principle may also be coded AI_UN_ROLE.

examples.quote: Artificial intelligence can improve, of course, education, health, agriculture, and public administration.

proposals.label: Global Digital Compact principles on AI
proposals.definition: Endorsement of the Global Digital Compact's principles on safe, secure and trustworthy AI for development.
proposals.inclusion: Passages welcoming Global Digital Compact or Pact for the Future provisions on AI.
proposals.exclusion: Non-UN governance references.
proposals.boundary_cases: If the GDC is named without any AI or technology content, do not code.

examples.quote: We welcome the Global Digital Compact’s principle of ensuring safe, secure and trustworthy emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence

proposals.label: Developing countries as passive AI consumers
proposals.definition: Concern that developing countries remain passive consumers of AI designed elsewhere and that the digital divide becomes a development divide.
proposals.inclusion: Passages warning that developing countries are mere consumers of foreign technology/algorithms or that AI opportunity without inclusion deepens inequality.
proposals.exclusion: Passages about AI benefits without an inequality dimension.
proposals.boundary_cases: Calls for 'digital sovereignty' framed around being left behind fit here; if framed as dependence on dominant powers, also code sovereignty.

examples.quote: The digital divide must not become the next development divide. Developing countries must not remain passive consumers of technologies designed elsewhere.
Developing nations must not be left behind as mere consumers or algorithms designed elsewhere.

proposals.label: Building capacity to co-create technology
proposals.definition: Calls for capacity in research, innovation and youth skills so developing countries become co-creators of technology.
proposals.inclusion: Passages calling for capacity to participate in research/innovation or for STEM and digital training to make youth co-creators.
proposals.exclusion: Generic education statements unrelated to technology.
proposals.boundary_cases: Youth STEM training in a digital-economy context may also be coded AI_YOUTH_EDUCATION.

examples.quote: We need the capacity to participate in research, innovation, entrepreneurship, and global technology governance.
We must equip our youth with STEM education, digital literacy, and technical training so they become co-creators in the global digital economy

proposals.label: Inclusive, responsible AI governance
proposals.definition: Calls for inclusive, responsible, cooperative governance and greater regulation of AI.
proposals.inclusion: Passages demanding inclusive AI governance, ethical norms or greater regulation.
proposals.exclusion: Passages only about national capacity.
proposals.boundary_cases: Support for the SG's scientific panel should also be coded AI_UN_ROLE.

examples.quote: the governance of artificial intelligence must be inclusive responsible, and grounded international cooperation

proposals.label: Support for UN scientific panel on AI
proposals.definition: Welcoming UN-specific AI governance mechanisms such as the SG's Independent International Scientific Panel on AI.
proposals.inclusion: Passages naming UN AI bodies or processes approvingly.
proposals.exclusion: Generic calls for regulation without UN reference.
proposals.boundary_cases: Mentions of UN reform unrelated to AI do not count.

examples.quote: Liberia welcomes global effort to govern new technologies including the Secretary General's independent international scientific panel on artificial intelligence.

proposals.label: Regulating AI in warfare
proposals.definition: Calls to regulate AI in warfare to prevent automated destruction.
proposals.inclusion: Passages referring to AI in warfare or automated destruction.
proposals.exclusion: Civilian AI regulation.
proposals.boundary_cases: General ethics calls that single out warfare count here.

examples.quote: greater regulation of artificial intelligence, particularly in warfare. Innovation must protect human development, not automate human destruction.

proposals.label: Militarization through autonomous weapons
proposals.definition: AI risks framed in terms of militarization, including autonomous weapons.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages naming autonomous weapons or militarization as an AI risk.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude general safety concerns about opaque models not linked to military use.
proposals.boundary_cases: Lists that include militarization among several AI risks count here as well as in other risk codes.

examples.quote: even militarization throughout autonomous weapons

proposals.label: Opaque models need safeguards before critical tasks
proposals.definition: Concern that poorly understood AI models should not be entrusted with critical tasks without robust safeguards, with catastrophic framing.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages about AI interpretability, safeguards for critical uses, or catastrophic outcomes from unsafe AI.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude military-only framing, which goes to AI_MILITARY_WEAPONS.
proposals.boundary_cases: Hyperbolic 'destroy the world' language tied to unsafe deployment counts here.

examples.quote: As long as we do not fully understand how these models work, we cannot entrust them critical tasks without robust safeguards in place.

proposals.label: Technology transfer and African AI capacity
proposals.definition: Calls for technology and knowledge transfer, investment in connectivity, compute, research and youth training so Africa is more than a supplier of minerals.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages requesting technology transfer, compute, training or partnerships to build AI capacity in developing/African states.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude climate finance requests without technology content.
proposals.boundary_cases: Framing about Africa not only supplying minerals for innovation hubs fits here and in AI_SOVEREIGNTY_CONCENTRATION.

examples.quote: We need to have investment in connectivity, computing capacity, scientific research, training of young people in Africa, technology transfer, governance, ethics for AI
through genuine transfer and sharing of knowledge, of technology

proposals.label: Africa beyond supplying minerals
proposals.definition: Concern that Africa remains a raw-material supplier to foreign innovation hubs, with calls for autonomy and African role in setting AI rules.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages asserting African agency in setting AI standards or rejecting a supplier-only role.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude general Security Council representation claims.
proposals.boundary_cases: Calls for Africa to define international AI rules also fit AI_GLOBAL_GOVERNANCE.

examples.quote: Africa must not limit itself to supplying the minerals that fuels the world innovation hubs
our continent, Africa, can and must play an active role in defining international roles and standards

proposals.label: Extraordinary opportunities, serious risks
proposals.definition: AI framed as offering extraordinary opportunities alongside exclusion, manipulation and other risks.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages pairing AI opportunities with explicit risks.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude one-sided statements.
proposals.boundary_cases: If specific risks (weapons, safety) are named, code those too.

examples.quote: Artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies offer extraordinary opportunities, but also serious risks of exclusion, manipulation of the society

proposals.label: Ethical, human-centred AI preserving human judgment
proposals.definition: Speaker insists AI must respect ethical boundaries, be transparent and human-centred, and complement rather than replace human judgment.
proposals.inclusion: Include calls for ethical, responsible, transparent or human-centred AI, or statements that AI must not substitute for human judgment.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude calls for global rules that do not reference ethics, human dignity or human roles.
proposals.boundary_cases: A call for a 'global standard' justified by ethics is coded both here and AI_GLOBAL_GOVERNANCE.

examples.quote: artificial intelligence must not be a substitute for human judgment or responsibility
We call for ethical, responsible, inclusive, and human-centered development and use of artificial intelligence with appropriate safeguard

proposals.label: Inclusive global standards for AI
proposals.definition: Speaker calls for global standards or an inclusive international framework governing AI and emerging technologies.
proposals.inclusion: Include calls for a global standard, international framework, or rules governing AI development and deployment.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude passages only praising AI's potential without any governance demand.
proposals.boundary_cases: If the emphasis is on who sets the rules (Africa, developing countries), also code AI_GLOBAL_SOUTH_VOICE.

examples.quote: We therefore call for a global standard that ensure that the usage of artificial intelligence remain transparent, fair for humanity.
We also call on the United Nations to continue to explore the creation of an inclusive international framework on emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence.

proposals.label: Developing countries shaping AI rules
proposals.definition: Speaker demands that Africa or developing countries have a stake and meaningful voice in setting AI rules and standards, often linking this to their supply of critical minerals.
proposals.inclusion: Include demands for African or developing-country participation in AI rule-making, including arguments based on critical minerals that power the technology.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude complaints about unequal access to AI without reference to rule-setting participation (code AI_DIGITAL_DIVIDE).
proposals.boundary_cases: Passages combining access inequality and rule-setting voice may take both this code and AI_DIGITAL_DIVIDE.

examples.quote: Africa must have a stake in shaping the rules that govern the development and the deployment of artificial intelligence
Developing countries must have a meaningful voice in setting the standards and safeguards that will govern these technologies

proposals.label: Youth as AI research and innovation force
proposals.definition: Speaker presents the country's or continent's young population as ready to contribute to AI research and innovation.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages linking youth or education to participation in AI research, innovation or skills.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude youth policy passages that do not mention AI.
proposals.boundary_cases: Youth training for other emerging industries without AI mention is excluded.

examples.quote: We have a youthful population ready to play a key role in the beneficiation at source of critical minerals and research and innovations for artificial intelligence.

proposals.label: AI as both opportunity and threat
proposals.definition: Speaker explicitly frames AI as presenting both opportunities and challenges or threats.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages that pair AI's benefits with its risks in an explicit dual framing.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude passages that mention only benefits or only risks.
proposals.boundary_cases: If the duality framing leads into a governance demand, also code AI_GLOBAL_GOVERNANCE.

examples.quote: artificial intelligence presents both unprecedented opportunities and profound challenges
the emergence of artificial intelligence, which presents both opportunities and threats to humanity

proposals.label: AI for development, productivity and SDGs
proposals.definition: AI is presented as a tool for accelerating development, productivity, agriculture, health, education and SDG achievement in developing countries.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages listing concrete development benefits of AI or linking AI to national development trajectory.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude passages in which AI is framed only as a risk.
proposals.boundary_cases: Brief mentions of harnessing 'science, technology, artificial intelligence' for development count here, possibly with AI_TECH_LIST_MENTION.

examples.quote: AI offers opportunities to strengthen agricultural productivity and food security, improve healthcare and education, enhance climate resilience
AI will usher in a new era of enhanced productivity for its citizens, helping to propel the country's development trajectory
harness the transformative potential of science, technology, artificial intelligence, and private sector development for national and global development

proposals.label: Inclusive, ethical global AI framework
proposals.definition: Speaker calls for a global framework for AI governance that is ethical, inclusive, development-oriented and accessible to all nations.
proposals.inclusion: Include explicit calls for a global or UN-promoted AI governance framework.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude general statements about AI benefits without a governance demand.
proposals.boundary_cases: Calls addressed specifically to the UN may also be coded AI_UN_ROLE.

examples.quote: We therefore call for a global framework that ensures AI is ethical, inclusive, and accessible to all nations
calls upon the United Nations to continue promoting an inclusive, ethical, and development-oriented global framework for AI governance

proposals.label: AI risks widening divides and job loss
proposals.definition: Speaker warns that unequal access to compute, data, infrastructure and skills, and automation-driven job disruption, may create a new technological divide for developing economies.
proposals.inclusion: Include warnings about AI deepening inequality between or within countries, including through labour disruption in fragile economies.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude generic references to inequality without an AI link.
proposals.boundary_cases: Passages focused only on employment effects without inequality should be coded AI_ECONOMY_LABOR.

examples.quote: Automation could disrupt employment and widen existing inequalities, while unequal access to computing capacity, data, digital infrastructure, skills, and financing risks creating a new technological divide

proposals.label: Human-centred AI complementing people
proposals.definition: AI should remain human-centred and complement rather than diminish human roles and dignity.
proposals.inclusion: Include statements that AI must be human-centred, safeguard human dignity, or complement human capabilities.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude passages that mention ethics only as an adjective in a governance call without elaboration.
proposals.boundary_cases: Calls for an 'ethical' framework alone lean to AI_GLOBAL_GOVERNANCE unless human-centredness is elaborated.

examples.quote: Artificial intelligence should complement and enhance human capabilities rather than diminish the indispensable role of people

proposals.label: Digital sovereignty: master, not consume AI
proposals.definition: AI framed through technological sovereignty: countries must master and adapt AI rather than merely consume it, as part of national sovereignty.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages asserting digital/technological sovereignty over AI or rejecting mere consumption of foreign AI.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude general access-gap statements without a sovereignty or control framing.
proposals.boundary_cases: National AI centres created explicitly to promote sovereignty also fit AI_NATIONAL_STRATEGY.

examples.quote: We must not simply consume AI technology. We must master it, adapt it to our realities, and contribute to its development.
digital and technological sovereignty has become an essential dimension of national sovereignty

proposals.label: Generative AI's opportunities and risks
proposals.definition: AI acknowledged as offering enormous opportunities but also significant risks.
proposals.inclusion: Include explicit framings of AI as both opportunity and risk.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude one-sided framings.
proposals.boundary_cases: Brief duality statements introducing sovereignty arguments still count.

examples.quote: AI offers enormous opportunities, and we acknowledge that, but also significant risks.

proposals.label: Investing in AI skills and infrastructure
proposals.definition: Need to invest in skills, research, innovation and infrastructure so youth can participate in AI transformation.
proposals.inclusion: Include calls to invest in AI skills, research, or infrastructure.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude generic education without AI.
proposals.boundary_cases: If investment is framed as youth participation, also consider AI_YOUTH_EDUCATION.

examples.quote: We must invest in skills, in research, in innovation, and infrastructure so that young people can participate fully in this transformation.

proposals.label: National AI and robotics centre
proposals.definition: The country cites establishing a national AI institution.
proposals.inclusion: Include references to national AI centres, strategies or investments.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude global calls.
proposals.boundary_cases: Also code sovereignty when explicitly linked.

examples.quote: has established Mali's Center for Artificial Intelligence Robotics to promote our country's digital sovereignty

proposals.label: Legal and ethical AI frameworks
proposals.definition: Call to define appropriate legal and ethical frameworks for AI.
proposals.inclusion: Include calls for legal/ethical frameworks for AI where not explicitly international.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude explicit international governance calls (AI_GLOBAL_GOVERNANCE).
proposals.boundary_cases: Ambiguous-level frameworks are coded here and may also get AI_GLOBAL_GOVERNANCE.

examples.quote: This requires defining and creating appropriate legal and ethical frameworks.

proposals.label: Who governs AI: few companies or countries
proposals.definition: Concern that a handful of private actors and a few countries control AI and set rules for everyone, and that the Global South becomes merely a data-centre destination.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages about private actors' control over communication and AI, or objections to a few companies/countries deciding AI rules.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude generic Security Council veto critiques without technology content.
proposals.boundary_cases: Complaints about data centres being placed in the Global South without decision power fit here and in AI_DIGITAL_DIVIDE.

examples.quote: the answer cannot be that small number of companies or countries decide the rules for everyone else
The global South cannot simply become a destination for data centers while decisions about AI are made elsewhere.

proposals.label: Global South participation in AI decisions
proposals.definition: Calls for the UN to empower Global South countries to participate in AI governance and share benefits equitably.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages demanding Global South participation, partnership rather than customer status, or equitable AI development.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude passages only about corporate power.
proposals.boundary_cases: Mentions of UN empowering the South also fit AI_UN_ROLE.

examples.quote: We must be partners in innovation, not merely customers and market, and not merely destinations for investment.

proposals.label: AI infrastructure demands on water and energy
proposals.definition: Concern about the resource demands (water, energy, land) of AI and tech infrastructure.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages discussing environmental or resource burdens of data centres/AI infrastructure.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude AI-for-climate solution claims (AI_DEVELOPMENT_SDGS).
proposals.boundary_cases: Energy supply for AI discussed purely as investment opportunity belongs to AI_NATIONAL_STRATEGY.

examples.quote: managing the enormous demands that tech infrastructure places on water, energy, land, and other resources

proposals.label: Governments failing to regulate AI abuse
proposals.definition: Criticism that governments choose not to regulate AI despite abuses, with calls for proactive governance and multilateralism.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages criticizing regulatory inaction on AI or calling for proactive governance.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude pure power-concentration arguments.
proposals.boundary_cases: Rhetorical questions such as 'who governs the transformation?' count here when followed by governance demands.

examples.quote: they are seeing their government choose not to regulate AI and the many ways it is being abused, but instead give it more power

proposals.label: Enormous opportunities and risks
proposals.definition: AI described as transforming economies and governance with both enormous opportunities and risks.
proposals.inclusion: Include explicit opportunity-risk pairings.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude one-sided statements.
proposals.boundary_cases: Short duality statements preceding a governance argument still count.

examples.quote: The opportunities are enormous. but also are the risks.

proposals.label: AI listed among emerging global challenges
proposals.definition: AI named alongside cybersecurity, terrorism, cybercrime or genetic engineering as a frontier or emerging issue, without further argument about AI itself.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages where AI is an item in a list of new challenges the UN or multilateralism must address.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude passages that describe specific AI governance tools, programmes or policy positions.
proposals.boundary_cases: Mention of 'economic disruption' from AI within such a list stays here unless the passage develops labour or economic effects.

examples.quote: the economic disruption caused by the emergence of digital technologies, including artificial intelligence and the potential for genetic engineering
Frontier issues such as artificial intelligence and cybercrime have leapt from the pages of science fiction into our daily lives.

proposals.label: AI as global commons needing common rules
proposals.definition: AI treated as a domain of the global commons requiring multilateral cooperation, common rules and trust-building, with rules framed as enabling rather than slowing progress.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages calling for multilateral commitment on AI as global commons or arguing that common rules and safeguards enable faster AI progress.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude passages only listing AI as a challenge without calling for cooperation or rules.
proposals.boundary_cases: Offering national governance frameworks and testing tools to others fits here and in AI_CAPACITY_BUILDING.

examples.quote: We need to bring the same constructive spirit to other areas of the global commons — AI, cybersecurity, digital technology and even outer space.
powerful engines and good brakes and common rules do not stop us or slow us down

proposals.label: Small-state AI capacity-building programmes
proposals.definition: Singapore offering capacity-building, governance frameworks and testing tools to small states and SIDS on digital technologies and AI.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages announcing training programmes, technical assistance, or sharing of AI governance tools with other states.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude domestic-only AI initiatives.
proposals.boundary_cases: Forum of Small States digital pillar activities count here when AI is explicitly or contextually included.

examples.quote: including Leadership and Governance in the Age of Digital Technologies and Artificial Intelligence
making our governance frameworks and testing tools available to all

proposals.label: Balancing AI innovation and regulation
proposals.definition: Call to find a balance between fostering AI innovation and regulating it, harnessing its potential while preventing harm to humanity.
proposals.inclusion: Passages explicitly calling for balance between innovation and regulation of AI.
proposals.exclusion: Unqualified calls for regulation or unqualified opposition to regulation.
proposals.boundary_cases: Balance framings that also name benefits and risks may be additionally coded duality.

examples.quote: we must find together the right balance between innovation and regulation

proposals.label: Harness potential while protecting human essence
proposals.definition: AI framed as both beneficial for humanity and capable of distorting human essence.
proposals.inclusion: Passages pairing AI's potential for humanity with a risk to human nature or values.
proposals.exclusion: Passages naming only benefits or only risks.
proposals.boundary_cases: Vague references to 'our very essence' count as the risk side.

examples.quote: harness its potential for the benefit of humanity, while preventing it from distorting our very essence

proposals.label: Extending international law to AI
proposals.definition: Extension of multilateralism and international law to new realities including AI.
proposals.inclusion: Passages calling for the legal extension of international law or multilateral frameworks to AI.
proposals.exclusion: Passages where AI is named without any governance/legal framing.
proposals.boundary_cases: Brief list items that still frame AI as a domain for legal extension count here and as list mention.

examples.quote: its legal extension to new global realities, such as the oceans, combating terrorism and artificial intelligence

proposals.label: New international rules for 4IR technologies
proposals.definition: The fourth industrial revolution, including AI and robotization, is said to demand new international rules of conduct and multilateral solutions.
proposals.inclusion: Include calls for new international rules or normative arrangements for AI and related technologies.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude passages mentioning AI only as a technology trend without rule-making demands.
proposals.boundary_cases: Where the UN is named as central rule-definer, also code AI_UN_ROLE.

examples.quote: the impact of new technologies — on the economy, the work world and relations among States — will demand new rules of conduct at the international level

proposals.label: UN central in defining technology rules
proposals.definition: The UN should play a central role in defining rules for new technologies by providing compromise solutions safeguarding the public interest.
proposals.inclusion: Include statements assigning the UN a central role in AI or tech governance.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude governance calls not referencing the UN.
proposals.boundary_cases: Generic UN centrality without technology context is not coded.

examples.quote: The UN must play a central role in defining them by providing compromise solutions capable of safeguard the public interest.

proposals.label: Fourth industrial revolution as challenge and opportunity
proposals.definition: The fourth industrial revolution including AI is framed as both a challenge and an opportunity, with effects on economy and work.
proposals.inclusion: Include explicit challenge-and-opportunity framings of AI or 4IR.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude one-sided framings.
proposals.boundary_cases: Mention of impacts on the 'work world' may also support AI_ECONOMY_LABOR.

examples.quote: What is know called the fourth industrial revolution presents both a challenge and an opportunity.

proposals.label: Regulating tech oligarchs controlling AI
proposals.definition: Speaker attacks the concentration of power in 'tech oligarchs' controlling social networks and AI development and calls for strict regulation of them.
proposals.inclusion: Include calls to regulate or curb powerful tech companies or individuals controlling AI.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude general governance calls not targeting corporate or state concentration of power.
proposals.boundary_cases: Calls for strict regulation of AI firms also warrant AI_GLOBAL_GOVERNANCE if framed internationally.

examples.quote: We must impose strict regulations on the tech oligarchs who control the functioning of social networks and the development of artificial intelligence.

proposals.label: Developing countries participating in AI governance
proposals.definition: Developing countries must actively participate in the governance and development of AI and emerging technologies.
proposals.inclusion: Include demands that developing countries take part in AI governance or development.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude access-only complaints without participation demands.
proposals.boundary_cases: A brief one-line demand in a list of reform priorities still counts here.

examples.quote: Developing countries must actively participate in their governance and development.

proposals.label: Keeping AI under human control
proposals.definition: Speaker insists AI, especially frontier models, must remain under human direction, oversight and control, and calls for mechanisms to control it.
proposals.inclusion: Passages stating humans must stay 'in the driver's seat' or that AI must remain under human oversight/control, or calling for mechanisms to control frontier AI models.
proposals.exclusion: General calls for AI regulation without the human-control framing (use AI_GLOBAL_GOVERNANCE); autonomous weapons human-control debates (use AI_MILITARY_WEAPONS).
proposals.boundary_cases: If the passage calls for international mechanisms to control frontier models, code both this and AI_GLOBAL_GOVERNANCE.

examples.quote: Artificial intelligence is developed by humans and must remain under human direction, oversight, and control.
Humans can and should be in the driver's seat.

proposals.label: Cooperative international governance of AI
proposals.definition: Calls for international cooperation, guardrails or joint initiatives among governments, companies and organizations to manage AI.
proposals.inclusion: Passages advocating multilateral cooperation, guardrails, or multi-stakeholder initiatives for responsible AI management.
proposals.exclusion: Mentions of UN internal modernization using AI (use AI_UN_ROLE) or generic multilateralism with no AI governance content.
proposals.boundary_cases: A national initiative launched jointly with other states to govern AI counts here, not as AI_NATIONAL_STRATEGY.

examples.quote: launched a call for companies, governments, regional organizations, and the UN to develop mechanisms to control frontier AI models
it requires guardrails so that it can be harnessed responsibly

proposals.label: AI as both promise and peril
proposals.definition: Explicit framing of AI as a transformative technology bringing both large opportunities and serious risks, often as civilization-scale change.
proposals.inclusion: Passages pairing AI's benefits with its dangers or describing it as the most consequential/transformative technology with major risks.
proposals.exclusion: Passages mentioning only benefits or only risks.
proposals.boundary_cases: Statements that AI's impact exceeds the industrial revolution count if paired with risk language.

examples.quote: Artificial intelligence brings enormous opportunities, but also incalculable risks for our civilization.
we must maximize the positive benefits of emerging technologies while curbing its darker potentials

examples.text: challenges, such as cybersecurity, counter-terrorism and the economic disruption caused by the emergence of digital technologies, including artificial intelligence and the potential for genetic engineering.

It is actually easy to understand why there is a resurgence in isolationist, protectionist and even xenophobic sentiments in the political arena all over the world. We are living in uncertain, volatile and disruptive times. The digital revolution is increasingly disrupting the way we live, work, play, communicate, organize and mobilize our societies. Non-State actors and transboundary threats, terrorism, pandemics and climate change remain a clear and present danger. Frontier issues such as artificial intelligence and cybercrime have leapt from the pages of science fiction into our daily lives. Our social cohesion is breaking down, and all too often we operate in isolated social and political bubbles.

Portugal welcomes and reaffirms its support for all the priorities that Secretary-General António Guterres has pursued in his coherent, dynamic and resolute mandate, including by defending effective multilateralism, based on international law and the Charter of the United Nations, and its legal extension to new global realities, such as the oceans, combating terrorism and artificial intelligence.

Secondly, new issues are emerging that demand multilateral solutions in accordance with normative and cooperative arrangements. What is know called the fourth industrial revolution presents both a challenge and an opportunity. From artificial intelligence and robotization to the implementation of smart grids and 5G infrastructure and data management, to restructuring entire sectors of the economy, the impact of new technologies — on the economy, the work world and relations among States — will demand new rules of conduct at the international level. The UN must play a central role in defining them by providing compromise solutions capable of safeguard the public interest.

We need to bring the same constructive spirit to other areas of the global commons — AI, cybersecurity, digital technology and even outer space. We do not lack policy ideas on strengthening multilateralism, but we need commitment and action. The High-level Advisory Board on Effective Multilateralism has put forward six transformational shifts that will make the United Nations and the multilateral system future-ready. For many small States, our survival and our very success require a strong United Nations and an effective multilateral system founded on the Charter of the United Nations and international law, and complied with by all States in the world. The Forum of Small States, chaired by Singapore, will continue to work with all States, large and small, to make the United Nations stronger and ready for the future.

Access to information in a universal, equitable and financially affordable manner, as well as to the instruments providing access to it, is also one of the major challenges of modern times. The Internet claims to represent a relationship of rapprochement between spaces and peoples, but the so-called spider web favours rich countries while developing countries are still poorly connected, particularly in Africa. At a time when the world and trade are becoming increasingly digital, it is becoming imperative for all countries to have access to the Internet, including artificial intelligence, which is revolutionizing the world as we speak. The increasingly widening and gaping abyss between the countries of the global North and the global South is causing the latter to lose a large number of social, scientific and economic opportunities. As leaving no one behind is one of the pillars of United Nations action, it is more than urgent that the digital divide be bridged in the legitimate interest of current and future generations.

In addition to facing security and climate challenges, the world is being shaped by a technological revolution for which few countries are prepared. Artificial intelligence holds great promise for our societies, but it can also pose a number of threats and lead to abuses, owing to the lack of international regulations governing its use. Consequently, it is incumbent upon us to ensure that that revolution does not exacerbate inequalities or lead to the digital disadvantage of part of humankind, but that, on the contrary, it promotes the progress and well-being of all. It is for that reason that my country welcomes the adoption of the Global Digital Compact (see resolution 79/1), which should enable better use of that technological advance, in the service of the progress of all nations.

The fourth International Conference on Small Island Developing States (SIDS4), held earlier this year, marked a significant milestone for all SIDS. We welcome the adoption of the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS, which outlines an action plan for the next decade. Singapore will support our friends in SIDS. We launched a new technical assistance package at SIDS4, called SIDS of Change, which covers priority areas, including blue carbon. Singapore will continue to support our fellow small States, and we will share our development experience. I am happy to announce that Singapore will renew our capacity-building programme for the Forum of Small States (FOSS). We have labelled that programme FOSS for Good, a package that will offer digital-themed programmes, including Leadership and Governance in the Age of Digital Technologies and Artificial Intelligence.

With the adoption of the Pact for the Future (resolution 79/1), including the Declaration on Future Generations and the Global Digital Compact, at the Summit of The Future, my Government is reinforcing its commitment to championing and investing in human capital development. Human capital development is a profound commitment to our people’s well-being and future. By investing significantly in education, healthcare and agriculture, my Government is laying the foundation for a prosperous and equitable Sierra Leone. Over the past six years, our achievements through our Free Quality School Education Programme, legislative reviews, governance reforms in the education sector and radical inclusion strategy have been highly impactful, well acclaimed and seen as a good model for the world. We welcome the Global Digital Compact’s principle of ensuring safe, secure and trustworthy emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, to offer new opportunities to accelerate development, leaving no one behind.

Given the world's unpredictable trajectory and the weakening of multilateralism, there is a pressing need, now more than ever, to restore the effectiveness of the United Nations on the basis of inclusive and equitable multilateralism. With this in mind, my country invites member states to reclaim the ideals enshrined in the UN Charter, as well as the constraints that fall to them as regards charter implementation. We call on member states to revive solidarity, solidarity which has always steered our actions. This is the collective commitment which will allow us, and of this I am certain, to tackle global challenges such as climate change, terrorism, scarce development financing, information wars, and regulation of artificial intelligence. Regarding the latter, a source of many hopes and fears, Cote d'Ivoire welcomes the adoption of the Pact for the Future and the annexes thereto, as well as the Global Digital Compact, regulating the use of artificial intelligence, AI. We call for the adoption of binding universal standards so as to regulate the use of AI and digital technologies to ensure that it is used to achieve development for the benefit of all. The UN's effectiveness during this critical period calls for, as a matter of priority, the completion of Security Council reform. The paralysis of this major organ consigns the United Nations and regional organizations to powerlessness. It pushes further away all prospects of peace and the lasting settlement of conflicts and the resolution of global challenges which threaten international peace and security. Now, more than ever, Security Council reform is vital for us to be able to adapt to new international realities and to strengthen the Security Council's legitimacy. Given the impasse which characterizes the negotiations process that's been underway for a number of decades, my country would like to reiterate its call for Security Council reform, which would, first and foremost, grant Africa its rightful place across all categories of this body, in keeping with the common African position expressed in the Izaruni Consensus and the Siut Declaration.

Hence, we call for a reform of its bodies, starting with its Security Council, this so as to make these bodies more representative, more transparent, and closer to the realities of our world. One can see clearly that the Security Council in its current composition no longer reflects the geopolitical balance of our world. Thus, the urgent need to reform it not in theory, but in practice. Africa cannot remain marginalized. This is a continent with more than 1,400,000,000 residents. It is a continent of the future, of the youth, of potential, for which today we need to ensure full and complete participation in global decision making. I wish to state forcefully, Africa deserves permanent representation on the United Nations Security Council, not as the beneficiary of a favor, but as a legitimate partner. This is the solemn call that the Republic of the Congo wishes to sound from this high rostrum. We must invent a smarter multilateralism, a more effective multilateralism, one that is closer to the aspirations of the people, and one that is more representative of the realities of the 21st century. This multilateralism also needs to be made manifest through concrete acts, through tangible results, and through sustainable solutions. The peoples of the world will not judge us by our speech, but rather by what we succeed in accomplishing together. Madam President, ladies and gentlemen, there can be no lasting peace without development, and the opposite is true as well. Poverty, inequality, youth unemployment, exclusion, This is the ground that produces frustration, instability, and violent extremism. We must honor our commitments for the financing of the Sustainable Development Goals and put an end to the machinery that strangles vulnerable economies. such as unsustainable debt or unfair trade rules. International solidarity remains vital to allow for developing countries to successfully weather their transition toward a more prosperous future. This is the reason why we need to invest massively in education, in health, agriculture, infrastructure, new technologies, artificial intelligence, inter alia. The climate is a very big challenge today. It goes beyond all borders, beyond all divisions.

For effective United Nations, it is necessary for the Security Council to be reformed to be more inclusive, accountable and responsible for maintaining international peace and security. The General Assembly must evolve into a representative policy-making body, rather than a debate club. The implementation of International Court of Justice judgments must become mandatory for all Member States, ensuring the rule of international law. Reform is needed not only for old challenges, but also for new ones. Artificial intelligence brings enormous opportunities, but also incalculable risks for our civilization. It is not just a technological leap. Its impact may be greater than the industrial and digital revolutions. Aware of this, my country and I support the proposal to make artificial intelligence a priority of the 80th session. Next year, we will elect a new Secretary-General of the United Nations. We need a person with leadership skills, with rich diplomatic experience, and ability to bring differences and build consensus, but also deeply humane and committed to the vulnerable. The next top diplomat of the world must possess knowledge, patience and tact. After 80 years, it is high time for a woman to be a Secretary-General of the United Nations. In a world dominated by strong men, often with weapons, we need strong women with wisdom and empathy. I believe that women, who along with their children are the greatest and most numerous victims of wars, have an inalienable right and obligation to prevent them. The anarchic international order is a threat to all, but especially to small states. It is natural for small and medium-sized states to be the greatest supporters of the United Nations reforms. Distinguished excellencies, let me share with you what we are doing in this regard. We supported the adoption of the Pact for the Future as a new global social contract. Living in one of the most climate vulnerable regions in the world, the Mediterranean, Macedonian citizens are already experiencing the consequences of the climate crisis, such as extreme weather conditions. That is why we supported the implementation of the Paris Agreement at COP26. 29 in Baku.

Artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies offer extraordinary opportunities, but also serious risks of exclusion, manipulation of the society, and even militarization throughout autonomous weapons. These advances pose new challenges to the defense and human dignity, justice, and labor. As long as we do not fully understand how these models work, we cannot entrust them critical tasks without robust safeguards in place. Otherwise, we are going to destroy the world. For that reason, Mozambique advocates a technological and climate diplomacy capable of regulating risk and democratizing benefits. through genuine transfer and sharing of knowledge, of technology, so that the science and technology are not factors of exclusion, but rather instruments of climate justice and inclusive development in the world. Faced with these interconnected challenges, our continent, Africa, can and must play an active role in defining international roles and standards, formulating principles and scientific ethics, and determining research priorities, ensuring that technology innovation is always at the service of the humanity and not the service of destruction of the humanity. In face of this crisis, the isolation is not the answer. Constructive dialogue and strengthening of multilateralism are. The Pact for the Future, adopted in 2024, offers concrete and innovative responses for relaunching of multilateralism adapted to challenges to the 21st century. Mozambique, as an African country with vast natural resources and unparalleled cultural wealth, has distinguished itself in the promotion and strengthening of democracy in the African continent. Since we moved forward with political pluralism, we've been working tirelessly to consolidate the foundation of a robust democratic system, holding regular and transparent elections that reflect the will of people and ensure that every Mozambican citizen has the voice and a say in the decisions that shape the future of our nation in Mozambique. Indeed, our presence in this podium is a result of a free and a transparent process of the Mozambican people from Rovuma to Maputo, from Zumbo to Indico, and in the diaspora. We have historically had an ongoing commitment to dialogue and building bridges between different political and social actors.

At this juncture, let me express gratitude to all cooperating partners, including the United Nations, who have supported our efforts and initiatives on women empowerment, helping us to end child marriages, to reduce early pregnancies, to increase school completion rates for girls, and to ensure that increasing numbers of women participate meaningfully in our nation's affairs. Madam President, humanity's progress is inseparable from global peace and security, for true stability can only be achieved when no one is left behind. Yet, we have fallen short in narrowing inequality as the gap between rich and poor nations continues to widen, and developing countries like Malawi struggle with limited fiscal space, limited technology transfer, low productivity, and limited participation in global trade. Last year, we adopted the Pact of the Future, reaffirming our collective commitment to inclusive, resilient, and sustainable global governance and development. The Republic of Malawi, therefore, calls on the international community to foster an environment that supports inclusive growth, ensuring that its benefits reach the most vulnerable. To realize this vision, we must strengthen trade and investment as engines of prosperity and harness the transformative potential of science, technology, artificial intelligence, and private sector development for national and global development. Madam President, climate change stands as the most critical existential threat of our era, with its adverse effects disproportionately impacting developing nations like Malawi. Despite contributing minimally to global greenhouse gas emissions, the Republic of Malawi endures some of the most severe consequences of climate change. The increasing frequency and intensity of severe droughts, catastrophic floods, and destructive cyclones jeopardize food security by disrupting agricultural production, displacing vulnerable communities, and threatening hard-won developmental advancements. The Republic of Malawi has lived with this reality. Erratic weather patterns threaten our agricultural backbone, pushing vulnerable communities into food insecurity and economic despair, conditions that are ripe for discord. It is therefore important that our discussion on peace must be intrinsically linked to climate resilience, sustainable agriculture, and food sovereignty. Sovereignty, just like peace, is threatened by food insecurity.

We therefore call for increased investment in early warning systems, climate-smart agriculture, and social safety nets. A world that is food secure is a world more peaceful. Considering these challenges, Madam President, the Republic of Malawi urgently calls for bold and accelerated climate action that includes the full and effective implementation of the Paris Agreement. This involves not only enhanced commitments to reduce emissions, but also significant scaling up of financial resources dedicated to climate adaptation, addressing loss and damage, and ensuring equitable access to sustainable technologies. The Republic of Malawi firmly believes that only through a collective sense of responsibility and international solidarity can we protect our planet and provide a sustainable future for our generations to come. Beyond various agreements and boardroom meetings, time for action is now. We must act decisively to safeguard both our environment and the livelihoods of those most at risk. Madam President, the global community also needs to work together to address public health issues. My delegation, therefore, applauds your office for the efforts that led to the adoption of the Political Declaration on the Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases and the Promotion of Mental Health and Well-Being. No nation has been spared from the impact of these two health issues, whose causes are numerous. The response to these issues requires concerted efforts and collaboration. It is, therefore, rather disheartening that the political declaration faced many hurdles during the negotiation process. My delegation wishes to appeal for shared commitment to address the issues and, indeed, all other emerging public health issues. Madam President, In this digital age, artificial intelligence presents both unprecedented opportunities and profound challenges. If harnessed responsibly, AI can accelerate development, improve health and education, and unlock economic growth. Yet, without clear governance, it risks deepening inequalities and undermining security. We therefore call for a global framework that ensures AI is ethical, inclusive, and accessible to all nations, enabling it to serve as a force for development rather than division.

The Republic of Malawi is optimistic that AI will usher in a new era of enhanced productivity for its citizens, helping to propel the country's development trajectory. Madam President, let me take this opportunity to express my gratitude to your office for convening a high-level plenary meeting to commemorate the 30th anniversary of the World Programme of Action for Youth. The youth make up a large proportion of the population of Malawi and, indeed, in Africa. They are an indispensable force for sustainable development. They are leaders, major actors and beneficiaries of investments and creators of wealth for today and tomorrow. It is for this reason that the government of Malawi developed the 2023-2028 National Youth Policy to demonstrate its commitment to place young people at the center of the national development agenda and to undertake reforms which support effective engagement of youth in policy development, implementation, and monitoring in all sectors. Two notable areas that the Republic of Malawi has proudly championed in relation to youth and development is the youth peace and security agenda and youth innovation and entrepreneurship. To that end, we are investing in education, vocational training, and meaningful political and economic participation of our youth. We have an inclusive national peace architecture that enables women and youth to participate as negotiators, mediators and community leaders. We have also created a Youth Innovation Fund that supports youth innovators and entrepreneurs to realize their dreams. We therefore urge the international community to create concrete pathways for youth inclusion in political and economic decision-making processes. Let us invest in their potential, not just fear their energy. To that end, the Republic of Malawi calls for investing for peace through a dedicated funding for youth-led peacebuilding. Madam President, in closing, the Republic of Malawi reaffirms its unwavering commitment to multilateralism and to the central role of the United Nations in addressing the pressing challenges of our time. But let us be clear. Noble mandates alone will not deliver results unless they are matched by the necessary resources, fairly allocated and predictably provided.

Namibia acknowledges the technological advance in all fields, but ethical boundaries must be respected. However, artificial intelligence must not be a substitute for human judgment or responsibility. We therefore call for a global standard that ensure that the usage of artificial intelligence remain transparent, fair for humanity. Youth unemployment, increased economic inequality, lack of adequate housing, quality education and healthcare, water, energy and debt distress are among the common challenges that no one country can address alone. Through multilateral cooperation, our collective action must ensure that we all forge ahead to make the world a better place and to work together on those challenges in line with our theme, "Better Together." Madam President, 30 years since the adoption of the Beijing Declaration and Platform of Action, we have much to celebrate and to ponder on. Namibia continues to make progress in the area of women participation in politics and decision-making. Currently, Namibia's cabinet has 57% of women. As we gear up to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the adoption of the UN Security Council Resolution 1325 on women, peace, and security, adopted during Namibia's presidency of the UN Security Council, Namibia will host two high-level events in Windhoek and New York. I look forward to the participation of all Member States in those events to collectively reaffirm commitment to the Women, Peace and Security agenda. And through the Namibia International Women Peace Centre, we will continue to advocate for the universal implementation of the Women, Peace and Security agenda. Madam President, we know to the ongoing efforts of the UN to ensure that we remain fit for purpose, including the UN8 initiative. We need an agile United Nations that is inclusive. Respect of the UN Charter and its purpose and principles must be our guiding star for our future endeavors. Madam President, we are meeting against a backdrop of profound global tension. The world is fractured by conflict, displacement, and economic instabilities, straining multilateral cooperation and a serious issue for us to reach consensus, a global liquidity crises threaten to plunge millions of people into poverty and insecurity.

We commend the role played by the elected members of the Council, which gives the wider membership of the UN greater agency in addressing the pressing issues of the day. We also believe it is important to strengthen the relationship between the Security Council and the General Assembly. We need a UN that delivers for real people on the ground. Clean water, education, pandemic preparedness, Social mobility, jobs, education, and an international financial architecture that delivers stability and prospects of progress for all, these are the building blocks for sustainable development and human dignity. The commitments made at the summit of the future last year signaled our collective resolve to implement the SDGs. The UN needs to be future ready and to harness the potential of emerging technologies like AI as a force for good for all. Early and constructive and inclusive multilateral engagement is essential, and AI's transformative force can aid conflict prevention, peacekeeping and humanitarian options. But you all know There are also downsides and dangers, and it requires guardrails so that it can be harnessed responsibly. Madam President, Excellencies, the first Foreign Minister of Singapore said it best 60 years ago in 1965, "Despite cynics who focus attention on its many shortcomings, Singapore has faith in the future of the United Nations, simply because without it, there is no worthwhile future for humanity." These words still ring true today. So together, let's ensure that this institution continues to serve as humanity's best hope for peace and prosperity for all of us. Thank you, Excellencies.

worsening inequality, debt levels which are reducing the room for maneuver available to many states, as well as climate upheaval, which is hitting the most vulnerable the hardest. At the same time, we're witnessing technological transformation on a vast scale. It's accelerating. AI is already transforming knowledge, work, our economies, education and information. Never has humanity had so many different means to shape its fate. However, nor has humanity ever been so acutely aware of the need to make collective decisions about how these means should be used to serve the common good. This is why the theme of this 81st session, Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation, a UN that delivers for all, resonates so strongly. The true challenge of our time is not just managing a succession of crises, but it is restoring our collective capacity to anticipate, to make decisions, to act. before these crises become irreversible. Mr. President, Benin believes in multilateralism. We believe not because we harbor nostalgia for the world of 1945, but because in 2026, the world more than ever needs a forum where states can talk to one another, listen to one another, and act in concert. Defending multilateralism also means taking a lucid look at the United Nations Organization. Trust, indeed, is not something you can order. It takes shape when our organization can respond to the expectations of our people, the people it serves, when the organization can deliver concrete results. It is in this spirit that Benin supports the efforts undertaken within the framework of the UN80 initiative. We need to achieve greater efficiency, coherence, transparency and responsibility. Nonetheless, we should remain cognizant of a key requirement. Reforming the UN doesn't simply mean cutting costs. What it should mean is boosting the organization's impact. A more effective United Nations should be better positioned to prevent conflicts, to respond to humanitarian crises, to shore up development, and anticipate the transformations which are already shaping our future. It should also remain true to the principles which underpin its legitimacy, universality, the sovereign equality of states, solidarity, and respect for the UN Charter.

In this regard, Botswana reaffirms its support for comprehensive Security Council reform and aligns itself with a common African position as articulated in the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration. We believe that a Security Council that continues to exclude Africa and Latin America from permanent membership cannot credibly claim to reflect contemporary geopolitical realities. We also call on the United Nations to continue to explore the creation of an inclusive international framework on emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence. We recognize technology as a bridge that narrows global inequality. This extends to critical minerals, rare earths, and energy resources that power the technological revolution, many of which come from developing countries. Therefore, Developing countries must have a meaningful voice in setting the standards and safeguards that will govern these technologies, ensuring that they expand opportunities, support decent work, and strengthen public services while protecting human dignity, rights, and security. Mr. President, I wish to reaffirm Botswana's commitment to multilateralism. We believe that shared challenges require shared solutions. We also believe that implementing the Pact for the Future, together with the UN80 initiative, offers an opportunity to translate our shared commitments into practical improvements in the functioning of the United Nations. In conclusion, Mr. President, I reemphasize that restoring trust Managing transformation and delivering for all are interconnected. We restore trust when we uphold our commitments, respect the UN Charter, and apply international law consistently. We manage transformation when change creates opportunity rather than deepens inequality, when developing countries have a meaningful voice in shaping the system that affect their future. And when technological and economic progress serve humanity as a whole. And we deliver for all when our decisions translate into tangible improvements in peace, security, development, health, and human dignity. The difference our decisions make in the lives and livelihoods of people is the standard against which the credibility of the United Nations must be measured. Botswana is ready to work with all member states. We may be small in size, but we are sturdy in principle.

But two years after its adoption, negotiations on Security Council reform are still ongoing. The decision so urgently needed has yet to be made. The African position, represented for years now by the Ezulwini Consensus and the Cirt Declaration, is not a favor we're asking. It is a demand for justice and effectiveness. Transformation next requires peacekeeping operations with realistic mandates and predictable financing. We support strengthening the UN-African Union partnership, including through predictable financing for African-led operations. Lastly, the transformation requires an international financial architecture that stops penalizing fragile countries. These reforms are not favors. They are investments in the world's stability. The UN must benefit all of its members. Mr. President, digital transformation and the rise of artificial intelligence are rightly considered to be one of the great promises of our time. The Global Digital Compact must become a reality. Affordable connectivity, skills transfer, data protection, and a governance of AI in which developing countries decide instead of simply being users. The transformation also requires facing history with lucidity. The wounds left behind by colonization are still being felt on our continent. Reparations are not simply reopening a feud of the past. They are a demand for justice for the future, recognition of the wrongs committed, restitution of cultural goods and archives, equitable cooperation, debt relief. There are many possible paths. The African Union has prioritized this, and the CEAR fully supports these efforts. Transformation calls for real respect for the sovereignty of states. Sanctions and restrictions must be tools for peace and must be adjusted in accordance with the progress made. They must not be retaliatory measures serving geopolitical interests. Mr. President, we are at a crossroads. We have our diagnoses. It is now time for decision. That is why the CAR calls upon the UN to act. Saving the world is not a task for one nation or one continent. It is our collective will to action that this 81st session be one in which we stop taking stock and begin taking action. Thank you for your kind attention.

The challenge now lies in our collective ability to mobilize them and to channel them with greater equity, solidarity, and effectiveness in the service of sustainable development. Cote d'Ivoire therefore calls for an ambitious reform of the international financial architecture and a renewed global partnership. to ensure that developing countries have more equitable access to the resources needed to finance infrastructure, health, education, energy, industrial transformation, and the creation of decent jobs for young people. Climate challenges require a similar degree of mobilization. Africa contributes the least to global greenhouse gas emissions, yet remains among the regions most hit the hardest by their consequences. Droughts, floods, land degradation, and the disruption of food systems directly threaten the ways of life and the livelihoods of millions of people. In this context, honouring international commitments on climate finance, adaptation and technology transfer is an imperative of justice and solidarity. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, the transformation that our world is experiencing is also a technological one. Artificial intelligence and the digital revolution are opening up considering opportunities in many areas of our contemporary world. However, these technological advances can also exacerbate existing divides if their development as well as access to them remain unevenly distributed. In this regard, Cote d'Ivoire supports the efforts of the United Nations to promote the global governance of artificial intelligence that fosters innovation while protecting human dignity, international security, and sustainable development in a spirit of inclusion, ethics, and equitable sharing of the benefits of technological progress. Mr. President, the trust that we seek at the international level must also be built within each of our states. through the strength of our institutions and our ability to create the conditions for sustainable and shared development. My country, for its part, under the leadership of President Alassane Ouattara, continues on its path towards a stronger and more diversified economy while taking care to ensure and safeguard peace and stability.

We reiterate the fact that we are available to accompany our brotherly countries in their work to achieve return to peace and stability. Through our history, we know that peace is difficult to build, but it is the only victory that benefits one and all. Ladies and gentlemen, your excellencies. guided by the same sense of responsibility. The recurring Ebola outbreaks and repeated pandemics have shown that global threats are no longer solely military or economic. Health security has become an essential component of collective security. And here, we will continue supporting the strengthening of the World Health Organization Regional Office for Africa in Brazzaville and will shoulder all of its responsibilities in accordance with the 1952 Headquarters Agreement. We also call for international governance of artificial intelligence in outer space. These technologies must remain in the service of humanity, progress, and the empowerment of peoples. Technological progress must not become a new instrument of domination. Africa must also be a center of creativity, innovation, and digital sovereignty. Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, to conclude, the Republic of the Congo remains faithful to its principles, peace, development, sovereignty, good neighborliness, dialogue, cooperation, and mutual respect amongst nations. We will continue to defend our national interests while fulfilling our international responsibilities. We will continue to believe in Africa and in our shared destiny, and we will continue to choose the United Nations as a privileged space for dialogue amongst people. I thank you.

And today, is one of those times and therefore it's our duty to rise to the courage and the ambition present in this text in the United Nations Charter and this is why ladies and gentlemen we need to reform the Security Council so that all of the regions in the world have fair representation and so that we can do away with the right of veto of the permanent members because as the UN Charter sets out no country should be judged in its own case, no matter how powerful they are. We therefore need to strengthen all of the other main bodies and reorganise the agency's funds and programmes and provide them with more resources and more executive capacity so that they can have a more decisive impact on the great challenges that beset humanity. We must strengthen bodies like the International Criminal Court so that they can investigate, prosecute and punish those that break the rules. It took humanity centuries to replace might is right with the rule of law, and we must not be the generation that backtracks on this. It's for this very reason that we must rebuild the nuclear non-proliferation and disarmament architecture to avoid a poorly designed security policy bring us back to another global conflict. We must impose strict regulations on the tech oligarchs who control the functioning of social networks and the development of artificial intelligence. At the end of the day, the future of our children is more important than the pockets of these tech oligarchs. Of course, doing all of these things will require compromise, time, strong leadership being able to build agreements, to listen, to look beyond our known reality and imagine a better alternative. And what I'm advocating for, for this leadership, is very clear. Nine men have served as Secretary General of this organization in its 80 years of existence. Now it's time for a woman to serve, a Latin American woman.

We have to make sure that international economic cooperation continues to be rules-based, legitimate, and representative. Multilateral solutions are needed in an increasingly multipolar world. We must also bring the United Nations back to peace mediation. The Secretary-General as mediator in chief will have a key role. The UN's legitimacy as a mediator is unique. Together, the UN and its member states can accomplish what neither can achieve alone. The UN needs to be at the center of rulemaking and institution building. Regional integration and thematic coalitions can and should support it. Now, let me finish by saying that artificial intelligence is the most consequential technology in the history of mankind. It will impact science, the economy, politics, security, and the very essence of our humanity. Humans can and should be in the driver's seat. We have a choice. We can compete, cooperate, or slow down. For me, cooperation is the best way forward. This is why Norway and Finland have, together with leaders from nations around the world, launched a call for companies, governments, regional organizations, and the UN to develop mechanisms to control frontier AI models. And I would really like for as many UN member states as possible to join this initiative. My country, Finland, wants the United Nations to succeed and will remain strongly engaged in its work. Therefore, we are standing for an election to the Security Council from 2029 to 2030. We are motivated by our belief in the UN Charter and the values it stands for. We will prioritize peace, people, and partnerships. We are willing to take on the responsibility of the Council membership at a time that calls for more peace. We want people and nations to thrive. We believe in dialogue and cooperation. Finally, let me make a procedural proposal. The foundations of the United States were built in San Francisco over 80 years ago. Today, we must restore balance to the world order. We must recommit to the fundamental principles of the international order, and we must embrace cooperation over conflict.

But we urge that our national ambition be supported by international action to make climate finance accessible, predictable, and adequate, including through the sustained implementation of the new collective quantified goal on climate finance and effective management to address loss and damage, build climate resilience, and a fairer international order in which those who have contributed least to the climate crisis are not left to bear the greatest burdens. Mr. President, artificial intelligence and emerging technologies offer extraordinary opportunities, but opportunity without inclusion can become another source of inequality.
